task: Connect the two blue Cat5e cables from the old phone block to new keystone jacks, join them with a patch cord, then test the link.

plan.job_title: Terminate Cat5e cables into keystone jacks
tools_needed: Punch-down tool (a small hand tool that pushes wire into a keystone jack slot and trims the excess — a 110-blade type fits Cat5e jacks)
Two Cat5e keystone jacks (the small snap-in sockets the cable plugs into)
One short patch cord (a pre-made Cat5e cable with RJ45 plugs on both ends, any length 1–3 ft)
Cable tester (a device with two ends: plug one end of the patch cord into each end to confirm all 8 wires connected correctly)

steps.title: Identify the two blue Cat5e cables
steps.action: Locate the two blue Cat5e cables currently punched into the existing phone distribution block (the black multi-port strip in the center of the panel). Trace each one to confirm it is a Cat5e cable and not a coax or phone line.
do_not_touch: coax splitter (the silver metal box at the top)
coax cables (the thick black cables with screw-on metal ends)
yellow-green wire at the bottom (this is a ground wire — leave it alone)
steps.stop_condition: If either cable feels warm, smells, or shows any scorching or melted insulation, stop and contact a professional.
steps.evidence_required: A photo clearly showing both blue Cat5e cables and where they enter the block, so the starting point is confirmed.
highlight_targets: two blue Cat5e cables entering the distribution block

steps.title: Unscrew or release each cable from old block
steps.action: Using the small flathead screwdriver, gently lever each blue Cat5e cable's wires out of the existing punch-down block terminals (the rows of colored wire slots). Work on one cable at a time.
do_not_touch: any wires belonging to the other cable while working on the first
steps.evidence_required: A photo showing the wires of one blue Cat5e cable fully freed from the old block, with the individual colored wire pairs visible.
highlight_targets: punch-down terminal slots holding the blue cable wires

steps.title: Trim and strip the first Cat5e cable end
steps.action: Cut the end of the first freed cable back about 1 inch (25 mm) to get a clean end, then strip (remove) the outer gray or blue jacket by about 1 inch to expose the four twisted pairs (eight thin colored wires inside).
do_not_touch: the four twisted pairs — do not untwist them more than needed yet
steps.evidence_required: A photo showing the first cable with roughly 1 inch of jacket removed, all four twisted pairs visible and intact.
highlight_targets: outer jacket of the first blue Cat5e cable

steps.title: Seat wires into first keystone jack using T568B order
steps.action: Following the color-code diagram printed on the keystone jack body, press each of the eight thin wires into the correct labeled slot in T568B order (the most common standard, usually marked on the jack). Keep each pair twisted as close to the jack as possible, then use the punch-down tool to press each wire firmly into its slot — you will hear a click and the tool trims the excess wire end.
do_not_touch: second blue Cat5e cable — leave it attached to old block until this jack is done
steps.stop_condition: If a wire snaps off inside the jack slot, discard that jack and start with a new one.
steps.evidence_required: A close-up photo showing all 8 slots of the first keystone jack filled with wires, with trimmed wire ends visible beside the jack.
highlight_targets: color-coded wire slots on the keystone jack

steps.title: Repeat strip and punch-down for second cable
steps.action: Repeat Steps 2, 3, and 4 for the second blue Cat5e cable: free it from the old block, trim and strip 1 inch of jacket, then punch all 8 wires into the second keystone jack in the same T568B color order.
steps.evidence_required: A photo showing both keystone jacks with all 16 slots (8 per jack) filled and wire trim ends visible beside each jack.

steps.title: Snap both keystone jacks into a surface mount or patch panel
steps.action: Press each keystone jack firmly into its port on a keystone surface-mount box or patch panel (the plastic housing designed to hold the snap-in jacks) until you hear a click and the jack sits flush.
do_not_touch: the punched-down wires on the back of each jack — do not flex them
steps.evidence_required: A photo showing both jacks clicked flush into their housing with no gaps around the edges.
highlight_targets: snap-in port on the mount or panel

steps.title: Connect the patch cord between the two jacks
steps.action: Plug one RJ45 end (the clear rectangular plug) of the short patch cord into the first keystone jack, then plug the other RJ45 end into the second keystone jack.
steps.evidence_required: A photo showing the patch cord plugged into both keystone jacks with the tab clips seated and no plug pulling out.
highlight_targets: port opening on each keystone jack

steps.title: Test the link with a cable tester
steps.action: Unplug the patch cord, connect one end to the MAIN port of the cable tester and the other end to the REMOTE port, then press the test button and watch the indicator lights (LEDs numbered 1–8) — all 8 lights must light in sequence with no skips or crosses.
steps.stop_condition: If any light stays off, lights out of sequence (a cross), or the tester shows a FAIL result, go back to the jack for that wire pair and re-punch the wires in the failing slot.
steps.evidence_required: A photo of the cable tester display or LED row showing all 8 lights lit in order (1–8) with no gaps, confirming a good end-to-end connection.
